blocks.body:
A farmer has $40$ metres of fence and wants a rectangular pen of the largest possible area. Sides $10 \times 10$ give $100$ square metres, $12 \times 8$ gives $96$, $15 \times 5$ gives $75$. The square wins, and the reason is a single inequality: for a fixed sum, a product of non-negative numbers is largest when the numbers are equal.

That inequality, the arithmetic mean–geometric mean (AM–GM) inequality, is the most used tool in elementary inequalities. This page proves it for any number of terms, shows how to apply it (the art is in choosing what to apply it to), and places it inside a whole ladder of means, the power means.

blocks.title: Two numbers
blocks.body:
For $x, y \ge 0$, the square $(\sqrt x - \sqrt y)^2$ is non-negative. Expanding,

$$x + y - 2\sqrt{xy} \ge 0, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \frac{x+y}{2} \ge \sqrt{xy},$$

with equality exactly when $\sqrt x = \sqrt y$, i.e. $x = y$.

There is also a picture. Draw a circle with diameter $AB$ and pick $P$ on $AB$ with $AP = x$, $PB = y$. The perpendicular to $AB$ at $P$ meets the circle at $Q$. Triangle $AQB$ has a right angle at $Q$, and the altitude from the right angle satisfies $PQ^2 = AP \cdot PB = xy$. A half-chord is never longer than the radius, so $\sqrt{xy} = PQ \le \tfrac{x+y}{2}$, with equality when $P$ is the centre.

For the farmer: if the sides are $a$ and $b$ with $a + b = 20$, the area is $ab \le \big(\tfrac{a+b}{2}\big)^2 = 100$, with equality only for $a = b = 10$.

blocks.title: AM–GM inequality
blocks.body:
For real numbers $x_1, \dots, x_n \ge 0$,

$$\frac{x_1+\cdots+x_n}{n} \ge \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n},$$

with equality if and only if $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n$.

Let $A = (x_1 + \cdots + x_n)/n$.

If some $x_i = 0$, the right side is $0 \le A$, and equality would force $A = 0$, i.e. all $x_i = 0$. So assume from now on that all $x_i > 0$.

If all the $x_i$ equal $A$, both sides equal $A$. Otherwise, since $A$ is their average, some $x_i$ is below $A$ and some $x_j$ is above it. Replace the pair $(x_i, x_j)$ by $(A,\ x_i + x_j - A)$. Three things happen:

1. The sum, hence the mean $A$, is unchanged.
2. The new numbers are positive, since $x_i + x_j - A > x_i > 0$.
3. The product of the pair goes up, because
$$A(x_i + x_j - A) - x_ix_j = (A - x_i)(x_j - A) > 0.$$
The other numbers are positive and untouched, so the whole product strictly increases.

Each such step makes at least one more entry equal to $A$. When $n - 1$ entries equal $A$ the last one does too (the sum is $nA$), so after at most $n-1$ steps every entry is $A$ and the product is $A^n$. The product only increased along the way, so the original product was less than $A^n$. Taking $n$-th roots: if the $x_i$ are not all equal, the geometric mean is strictly less than $A$.
blocks.title: Proof by smoothing
Weighted AM–GM
blocks.body:
Often the terms deserve different weights. If $w_1, \dots, w_n \ge 0$ with $w_1 + \cdots + w_n = 1$ and $x_i \ge 0$, then

$$w_1x_1 + \cdots + w_nx_n \ge x_1^{w_1}x_2^{w_2}\cdots x_n^{w_n}.$$

For rational weights this is ordinary AM–GM in disguise. Write $w_i = m_i/N$ with whole numbers $m_i$ and apply AM–GM to $N$ numbers consisting of $m_i$ copies of $x_i$. For instance, with two copies of $a$ and one of $b$,

$$\frac{2a + b}{3} = \frac{a + a + b}{3} \ge \sqrt[3]{a^2 b}.$$

Irrational weights follow by approximating with rational ones, or directly from the concavity of the logarithm (see [[convexity]]). As before, equality holds exactly when all $x_i$ with positive weight are equal.

blocks.title: How to use it: make the product constant
blocks.body:
AM–GM turns a sum into a product. It is useful when the product is something you control, typically a constant.

Minimise $x + \tfrac4x$ for $x > 0$. The two terms have product $4$, so $x + \tfrac4x \ge 2\sqrt{4} = 4$, with equality when $x = \tfrac4x$, i.e. $x = 2$. Since equality is attained, the minimum is $4$.

The equality case is also a guide. Before splitting terms, guess where the extremum is, then split so that all the pieces are equal there. Example 2 below shows a case where the naive split fails.

blocks.title: Power means
blocks.body:
For positive reals $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and a real number $p \ne 0$, the power mean of order $p$ is

$$M_p(x) = \Big(\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum x_i^p\Big)^{1/p},$$

and $M_0(x)$ is defined to be the geometric mean $\sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$. Special cases: $M_1$ is the arithmetic mean, $M_2$ the quadratic mean (root mean square), and $M_{-1} = n/(\tfrac1{x_1} + \cdots + \tfrac1{x_n})$ the harmonic mean. As $p \to +\infty$, $M_p \to \max x_i$, and as $p \to -\infty$, $M_p \to \min x_i$.

Taking the geometric mean as $M_0$ is not arbitrary: $M_p(x) \to \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$ as $p \to 0$, so it fills the gap continuously.

blocks.title: Power mean inequality
blocks.body:
For positive reals $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the power mean $M_p(x)$ is increasing in $p$: if $p < q$ then $M_p(x) \le M_q(x)$, with equality only when all $x_i$ are equal. In particular

$$\min x_i \le \frac{n}{\sum 1/x_i} \le \sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n} \le \frac{\sum x_i}{n} \le \sqrt{\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}} \le \max x_i.$$

The middle inequality GM $\le$ AM is AM–GM.

AM $\le$ QM: with $A = \tfrac1n\sum x_i$,
$$0 \le \frac1n\sum (x_i - A)^2 = \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - 2A\cdot A + A^2 = \frac1n\sum x_i^2 - A^2.$$

HM $\le$ GM: apply AM–GM to the numbers $1/x_i$: $\tfrac1n\sum \tfrac1{x_i} \ge \big(\prod \tfrac1{x_i}\big)^{1/n}$, and take reciprocals of both sides.

The two outer inequalities hold because every mean of the numbers lies between the smallest and the largest. Equality in each step forces all $x_i$ to be equal.

The general statement for arbitrary $p < q$ is a consequence of Jensen's inequality and is proved on the [[convexity]] page; we do not repeat it here.
blocks.title: Proof of the chain

blocks.body:
Prove that for all $a, b, c \ge 0$,
$$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) \ge 8abc.$$
When does equality hold?
blocks.solution:
By AM–GM for two numbers, $a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}$, $b + c \ge 2\sqrt{bc}$, $c + a \ge 2\sqrt{ca}$. All six sides are non-negative, so we may multiply:

$$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) \ge 8\sqrt{ab\cdot bc\cdot ca} = 8abc.$$

If $a, b, c > 0$, equality needs equality in each factor, so $a = b = c$. If some variable is $0$ the right side is $0$, and the left side is $0$ only when two of the variables vanish. So equality holds exactly when $a = b = c$ or at least two of $a, b, c$ are zero.

blocks.body: Find the minimum of $f(x) = x^2 + \dfrac{16}{x}$ for $x > 0$.
blocks.solution:
The naive two-term AM–GM gives $x^2 + \tfrac{16}{x} \ge 2\sqrt{16x} = 8\sqrt x$, which depends on $x$ and so proves nothing about the minimum.

The product must be constant. Since $x^2$ has degree $2$ and $\tfrac1x$ degree $-1$, split the second term in two:

$$x^2 + \frac8x + \frac8x \ge 3\sqrt[3]{x^2\cdot\frac8x\cdot\frac8x} = 3\sqrt[3]{64} = 12.$$

Equality requires $x^2 = 8/x$, i.e. $x^3 = 8$, $x = 2$, and indeed $f(2) = 4 + 8 = 12$. So the minimum is $12$, attained at $x = 2$. (Calculus agrees: $f'(x) = 2x - 16/x^2$ vanishes at $x = 2$.)
blocks.title: Splitting terms with the equality case in mind

blocks.body:
Prove that for $a, b, c \ge 0$,
$$a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \ge a^2b + b^2c + c^2a.$$
blocks.solution:
Each term on the right is a weighted geometric mean of cubes: $a^2b = (a^3)^{2/3}(b^3)^{1/3}$. Weighted AM–GM with weights $\tfrac23, \tfrac13$ gives

$$\frac{2a^3 + b^3}{3} \ge a^2b,\qquad \frac{2b^3 + c^3}{3} \ge b^2c,\qquad \frac{2c^3 + a^3}{3} \ge c^2a.$$

Adding the three, the left sides total $\tfrac{3(a^3+b^3+c^3)}{3} = a^3 + b^3 + c^3$. Equality needs $a = b = c$.

The pattern generalises: to bound a monomial such as $a^2b$ by a sum of pure powers, read off the weights from its exponents.
blocks.title: Weighted AM–GM

blocks.body:
Positive reals $a, b, c$ satisfy $abc = 1$. Prove that
$$a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge a + b + c.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $s = a + b + c$. Two rungs of the ladder are needed.

QM $\ge$ AM, squared and multiplied by $3$: $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge \tfrac{s^2}{3}$.

AM $\ge$ GM: $\tfrac s3 \ge \sqrt[3]{abc} = 1$.

Combining, $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \ge \tfrac{s^2}{3} = s\cdot\tfrac s3 \ge s$, which is the claim. Equality throughout forces $a = b = c$, and with $abc = 1$ that means $a = b = c = 1$.

Notice the role of the constraint: the inequality is not homogeneous (the two sides have different degrees), and $abc = 1$ is what lets AM–GM bridge the degree gap.
blocks.title: Climbing the ladder of means

blocks.body:
- Non-negativity matters. $x + \tfrac1x \ge 2$ is false for $x = -1$, and $\sqrt[n]{x_1\cdots x_n}$ need not even make sense for negative numbers.
- A bound is only a minimum if the equality case is allowed. For $x \ge 2$, AM–GM still says $x + \tfrac1x \ge 2$, but equality needs $x = 1$, which is excluded; the true minimum on $[2, \infty)$ is $\tfrac52$, at $x = 2$.
- If the product of the terms is not constant (as in the naive attempt on $x^2 + 16/x$), AM–GM gives a bound that depends on the variable, which usually proves nothing.
- Power means of order $p \le 0$ require all $x_i > 0$; for $p > 0$ zeros are allowed.

The inequality AM $\le$ QM is the simplest case of [[cauchy-schwarz]], and the general power mean inequality and weighted AM–GM are both instances of Jensen's inequality for convex functions ([[convexity]]). Muirhead's inequality, met in [[symmetric-ineq]], is a far-reaching generalisation of AM–GM for symmetric sums.

In geometry AM–GM gives the isoperimetric property of the equilateral triangle ([[geo-inequalities]]). By Heron's formula a triangle with sides $a, b, c$ and semiperimeter $s$ has area $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$. The three numbers $s-a$, $s-b$, $s-c$ are positive with sum $s$, so their product is at most $(s/3)^3$, giving

$$\text{Area} \le \frac{s^2}{3\sqrt3},$$

with equality only for the equilateral triangle: among triangles of a given perimeter, the equilateral one encloses the most area.

1. Prove that $x^4 + y^4 + 8 \ge 8xy$ for all real $x, y$.
2. Positive reals $a, b$ satisfy $a + b = 1$. Find the minimum of $\big(1 + \tfrac1a\big)\big(1 + \tfrac1b\big)$.
3. Prove AM–GM in another way, using $e^t \ge 1 + t$: apply it with $t = x_i/A - 1$ and multiply the results.
4. Show that $\sqrt[3]{abc} \ge \dfrac{3}{1/a + 1/b + 1/c}$ for positive $a, b, c$ without quoting the power mean inequality.
